common_name: Wintergrazer 70 Rye (High-Forage Southern Grazing & Cover Crop Rye)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in fall as soil cools; Wintergrazer 70 was selected through University of Georgia and USDA-ARS breeding work for rapid regrowth after repeated clipping or grazing, so it tolerates an earlier first cutting than many other winter ryes.

directions: Wintergrazer 70 is a forage-type cereal rye bred for exceptional winter cold tolerance combined with vigorous tillering that lets it bounce back quickly after grazing or mechanical clipping, making it a favorite dual-purpose forage-and-cover planting across the Southeast. Drill or broadcast into a prepared seedbed in fall; germination proceeds even in quite cold soil, and top growth continues slowly through mild winter spells. Where used strictly as cover, let the stand grow uninterrupted into a tall, fibrous mat that can be roll-crimped or mowed ahead of a no-till summer crop for weed suppression and organic matter. Its extensive root system also scavenges residual nitrogen and helps rebuild soil structure in compacted fields.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Cover Crop Species Guides

common_name: Bonel Rye (Nematode-Suppressive Southern Winter Cover Crop Rye)

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall; Bonel is a Southern-bred winter rye grown alongside Elbon as a root-knot-nematode-suppressive rotation crop ahead of susceptible vegetables.

directions: Bonel is a cereal rye cultivar developed for the Gulf South and mid-South alongside Elbon rye, sharing its role in vegetable rotations aimed at suppressing root-knot nematode populations ahead of nematode-susceptible crops like tomato and pepper. Broadcast or drill into a firm fall seedbed; the crop germinates in cold soil and grows steadily through mild Southern winters, tillering into a dense stand. Rye's root exudates and residues, rich in allelopathic benzoxazinoid compounds, help suppress weed germination and have been associated with reduced nematode pressure in following crops. Terminate by rolling, mowing, or incorporating two to three weeks before the next planting to allow residue to begin breaking down.
sources: SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) — Cover Crop Chart

common_name: Maton II Cereal Rye (Improved Texas-Bred Winter Cover & Grazing Rye)

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall; Maton II is a Texas A&M-improved successor to the original Maton rye, bred for stronger leaf disease resistance while keeping Maton's early maturity and grazing tolerance.

directions: Maton II is a Texas A&M AgriLife release bred as an improved successor to the original Maton cereal rye, targeting better resistance to leaf rust and other foliar diseases that could limit Maton's forage yield in humid Texas winters. Drill or broadcast into a firm seedbed in fall, where it establishes quickly and tillers into a dense winter stand suited to both grazing and cover crop use. Its earlier maturity than many northern rye types allows earlier spring termination ahead of a following cash crop, while its deep, fibrous roots build soil structure and scavenge nitrogen against winter leaching. Graze or mow periodically for forage, or let it grow to full height and roll-crimp at boot stage for a heavy no-till mulch.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Cover Crop Species Guides

common_name: Paradana Balansa Clover (Classic Early-Flowering Waterlogging-Tolerant Balansa Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill shallowly in fall; Paradana was one of the first widely marketed balansa clover cultivars, selected in Australia for early flowering and tolerance of temporarily waterlogged or acidic soils.

directions: Paradana is a historically important balansa clover cultivar bred in Australia and adopted early on by Southern US no-till growers looking for a fast, cool-season nitrogen-fixing cover legume. Sow seed shallowly onto a firm, moist seedbed in fall, since fine-seeded balansa clover establishes best with good seed-to-soil contact rather than deep burial. Paradana flowers earlier than many later-released balansa cultivars, letting growers terminate and plant a following crop sooner, and it tolerates brief spells of waterlogged soil better than most other annual clovers. Its dense, low winter growth suppresses weeds and its abundant hard seed allows a stand to reseed itself for several following seasons if allowed to mature.
sources: SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) — Cover Crop Chart
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Fact Sheets

common_name: Bolta Balansa Clover (Tall High-Biomass Winter-Active Balansa Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill shallowly in fall; Bolta is a taller, more winter-active balansa clover cultivar than older selections such as Paradana, giving it greater biomass for weed suppression and nitrogen contribution.

directions: Bolta is an Australian-bred balansa clover cultivar selected for taller growth and stronger winter activity than earlier balansa releases, giving it more forage and cover-crop biomass over a similar planting window. Broadcast or drill seed shallowly into a firm, moist fall seedbed, since the fine seed needs good soil contact rather than deep placement to establish reliably. Its taller, more upright habit makes it suitable for hay or silage in addition to cover crop use, and like other balansa types it tolerates brief waterlogging better than red or white clover. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or incorporation before or at early flowering to capture peak nitrogen content ahead of a following crop.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Fact Sheets
SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) — Cover Crop Chart

common_name: Cadiz Serradella (Soft-Seeded French Serradella Cover Crop)

planting.note: Sow in fall once soils cool below about 75F; Cadiz is a soft-seeded French serradella cultivar bred in Western Australia for easier same-season establishment than older hard-seeded serradella types, and benefits from an Ornithopus-specific rhizobium inoculant.

directions: Cadiz is a Western Australian-bred French serradella cultivar selected for a much lower proportion of hard (dormant) seed than traditional serradella, allowing a stand to establish reliably in its first season rather than lying mostly dormant like older ecotypes. Sow shallowly into a firm seedbed in fall using rhizobium-inoculated seed, since serradella nodulates poorly without the correct inoculant, especially on land where it has not previously grown. It thrives on the acidic, sandy, low-fertility soils where clovers and vetches often struggle, producing fine, fern-like foliage that fixes nitrogen and covers ground through winter and spring. Mow or incorporate before summer heat sets in, or allow a small amount of pod set for natural reseeding in orchard or vineyard alleys.

common_name: Coker 227 Oat (Classic Southern Winter Forage & Cover Crop Oat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early to mid-fall; Coker 227 is a long-standing Southern winter oat bred by Coker's Pedigreed Seed Company for improved cold tolerance and forage yield compared to typical spring oat types.

directions: Coker 227 is a historically important Southern-bred winter oat that for decades served as a benchmark cultivar in regional forage and cover crop variety trials, prized for surviving mild Southern winters better than ordinary spring oat seed. Drill or broadcast into a prepared bed in early to mid-fall so plants establish a solid stand before the coldest weather, then resume vigorous growth in late winter. It produces abundant, palatable forage for grazing or hay while also functioning as a fast-growing winter cover that suppresses weeds and protects soil from erosion. In colder zones outside its adapted range it will winterkill like other oats, leaving an easily managed mulch ahead of spring planting.

common_name: Empire Birdsfoot Trefoil (Classic Broad-Leaved Pasture & Cover Trefoil)

planting.note: Sow shallowly into a firm seedbed in spring using fresh, inoculated seed; Empire is one of the earliest widely commercialized birdsfoot trefoil cultivars in North America and remains a benchmark broad-leaved type in variety comparisons.

directions: Empire is a broad-leaved birdsfoot trefoil cultivar that became one of the earliest standard commercial trefoil types in North America and is still referenced as a benchmark in long-term pasture and cover crop research. Sow shallowly into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring with seed inoculated for the specific Lotus-associated Rhizobium strain, since establishment is slow and seedlings compete poorly with weeds in their first weeks. Once established it forms a long-lived, non-bloating forage and nitrogen-fixing cover suited to soils too wet, acid, or infertile for alfalfa or clover. Mow occasionally the first season to knock back competing weeds, after which the deep-rooted stand persists and builds soil fertility for several years.

common_name: Dawn Birdsfoot Trefoil (Cornell-Bred Vigorous-Seedling Pasture & Cover Trefoil)

planting.note: Sow shallowly into a firm seedbed in spring using fresh, inoculated seed; Dawn is a Cornell University-released birdsfoot trefoil cultivar selected for stronger seedling vigor and better crown health than older cultivars.

directions: Dawn is a birdsfoot trefoil cultivar released by Cornell University and selected for faster, more vigorous seedling establishment along with improved resistance to crown and root rot compared with older Northeastern trefoil cultivars. Sow shallowly in spring into a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed with properly inoculated seed, since even improved trefoil cultivars establish more slowly than clover and need reduced weed competition early on. Once its taproot system develops, Dawn provides long-lived, non-bloating grazing forage and a nitrogen-fixing perennial ground cover well suited to wet, acidic, or low-fertility soils where alfalfa performs poorly. It tolerates periodic mowing or light grazing and continues contributing biomass and fixed nitrogen for multiple growing seasons.
